item.itunes:summary:
Nvidia's RTX Spark platform is here, and we've been testing it in laptops since launch. Doing silly things like playing Minecraft with a local LLM or emulating games, and seeing how it measures up against AMD's Strix Halo. It's been great fun, but now it's time to play with a different form factor. RTX Spark mini PCs are now out, and I've been putting an MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ with 128GB of RAM and 4TB of SSD through its paces.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

For local LLM work, the large amount of unified memory makes this a compelling platform for developers who want to stay on Windows. And with the better cooling in the mini PC form factor, it lets the RTX Spark chip run at full whack.

About this review: Nvidia provided XDA with the MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ used in this review. Neither company had any input into its contents, nor saw it before publication.

  • No ConnectX-7 networking
$8000 at Official Site See at NVIDIA

Price, specs, and availability

The Nvidia RTX Spark mini PC is available as of today, November 18. Unlike the DGX Spark, there aren't any OEM Nvidia versions. Instead, you can choose from Asus, Dell, and MSI right now, with Acer, Gigabyte, HP, and Microsoft bringing their versions soon. It's the desktop version of the RTX Spark laptops that have been out for a month or so, with a 20-core Nvidia Grace CPU, Nvidia Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores, and up to 128GB of unified memory for local AI stacks to take advantage of.

The price depends on which company you get one from. The MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ we got for review has 128GB of RAM, 4TB of Gen5 SSD, and an eye-watering price tag of $8,000. The Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box has 128GB of RAM and a 2TB SSD for $6,000.

We've extensively covered the RTX Spark chips in other devices, from running Crysis in RAM to talking about how Windows on Arm can mix native and emulated code. The RTX Spark is faster than AMD's Strix Halo, and by no small measure either, so if you're trying to render assets in the shortest time, the MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ (or any other RTX Spark device) will pay for itself in time saved. No, it's not a gaming behemoth. It's not made to be, but being able to run Windows games (even those that need anti-cheat) is a blessing. And it's super quiet. By  Adam Conway

What I didn't like about the RTX Spark mini PC

It makes less sense as a mini PC

Here's the thing. RTX Spark laptops are also similarly expensive, but you get a keyboard and a nice screen, and speakers, and everything else you need to watch movies, play games, and keep an eye on your agents. Now, you don't need those things if you're running the RTX Spark as a headless device, but then you might be better off with the DGX Spark. Windows has never been a fun operating system to operate remotely.

The other annoyances I had are minor. The USB-C ports are all 20 Gbps, when they could be 40 Gbps USB4 ports. There's no USB-A port, no ports on the front of the device, and you lose the speedy ConnectX-7 networking ports the Linux-based DGX Spark boxes have. The 10 GbE networking port is good for a single machine, so Nvidia clearly doesn't expect people to cluster the RTX Spark boxes. And if it's being marketed to creatives, an SD card reader would have gone a long way.

Nvidia RTX Spark takes on AMD Strix Halo, and AMD has reason to worry

The head-start CUDA gives is hard to ignore

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Should you buy the Nvidia RTX Spark mini PC?

You should buy the Nvidia RTX Spark mini PC if:

  • You want to do AI or local LLM development on Windows
  • You need up to 128GB of VRAM
  • You want to play games as well

You should NOT buy the Nvidia RTX Spark mini PC if:

  • You want a better value mini PC
  • You prefer using macOS
  • You want RTX Spark power in a laptop instead

Nvidia clearly wants to position the RTX Spark mini PCs as a stay-at-home device while your RTX Spark laptop goes with you, chugging through agentic long-tail tasks unsupervised. And for the most part, it can deliver on that promise. I'm hooked on running local agents, fully offline, with the added privacy that creates, and my workflow has changed as a result. Being able to run research tasks overnight while I sleep is a boon, and that's only one thing that these local AI boxes can accomplish.

item.itunes:title: TP-Link's 8-port PoE Switch drops to $50 as part of a Black Friday deal
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Every camera or access point you add to a home network tends to come with another power brick and another hunt for a free outlet. Power over Ethernet (PoE) reduces that by sending power and data over the same cable, but your switch has to supply the power. The TP-Link LS108GP is $49.99 on Amazon right now, down from $59.99, as part of a Black Friday deal.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
TP-Link LS108GP
Dimensions
6.2 × 3.9 × 1.0 in (158 × 99 × 25 mm)
Weight
1.5 lb

The TP-Link LS108GP is an unmanaged 8-port Gigabit desktop switch in which all eight ports supply PoE+. It has a 62W total PoE budget with up to 30W per port, 16 Gbps switching capacity, and an Extend Mode that reaches up to 820 ft (250 m).

See at Amazon

Plenty of PoE for the money

Eight PoE+ ports in a desktop switch

All eight ports on the LS108GP supply PoE and are IEEE 802.3af/at compliant, so there's no split between powered and unpowered ports to plan around. You can send data and power over one Ethernet cable to compatible gear like cameras or access points, which means each device needs a cable run rather than an outlet beside it.

You get a total PoE budget of 62W, with up to 30W per port. Keep in mind that the 62W is shared across all eight ports, so add up the current draw of your devices before you fill every slot. Two devices pulling the full 30W would use 60W of that budget, leaving just 2W for the other six ports.

For data, you're looking at eight 10/100/1000 Mbps RJ45 ports, so a PC or other wired device can run at gigabit speeds. The switch has a 16 Gbps switching capacity, an 11.9 Mpps packet forwarding rate, a 4K MAC address table, and 16KB jumbo frames, which suit a small home office or a handful of security cameras.

Ports 1 and 2 also have an Extend Mode, which carries PoE power and data up to 820 feet. That could help if a camera sits in a detached garage or at the far end of a yard. The catch is that ports in this mode drop to 10Mbps, so it suits a far-off device that doesn't need much bandwidth rather than a PC. Only those two ports offer it, though PoE is available on ports 1 through 8, so every port can still power a device in its normal mode.

item.itunes:title: The best window manager for Windows is a free Microsoft tool most people have never installed
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Juggling windows on your computer can be a hassle with the default controls Windows 11 gives you. Snap Layouts are definitely a big improvement over how Windows used to handle multiple windows, but it's still just too restrictive in terms of options and how you can use them.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Enter PowerToys, a tool published by Microsoft that makes managing your open apps much easier. Despite being made by Microsoft, most of its features are still not built into Windows 11 today, so if you haven't yet, I highly recommend installing it as soon as possible. I can't use a Windows 11 PC without it.

Why Snap Layouts still isn't good enough

It's still too rigid

With Windows 11, Microsoft greatly improved window management compared to previous versions with the introduction of Snap Layouts. It builds on many of the improvements in Windows 10 and takes them further.

Not only can you snap apps into quadrants now, you can actually see additional layout options when you hover over the restore/maximize icon for a window, and that includes some brand-new options. You can have one app take half of the screen, while two others take the remaining quadrants, or use a three-column design with one app in each. Not only are there some new layouts, but they're easier to access, both through the aforementioned menu or by dragging a window to the top of the screen, which makes this work with touch, too.

4 Windows 11 tiling managers that put Microsoft’s Snap Layouts to shame

Upgrade your productivity

1
By  João Carrasqueira

However, these are still fairly limited options, and on top of that, moving a window into the right area takes too many extra steps. You have to either drag a window along the edges to snap it into the right position or open the layout picker to select where it needs to go. It's not a lengthy process, but that time does add up.

FancyZones turns it up to the max

Absolute freedom

This is where PowerToys, and specifically FancyZones, comes in and makes everything much better. It's actually somewhat surprising that this isn't part of Windows 11 itself considering Microsoft makes this tool, and I've been saying that should change for years at this point.

FancyZones addresses my two biggest complaints flawlessly. First, the customization options. Instead of limited preset layouts, FancyZones lets you customize the layouts you want down to the pixel. You can add areas, split them vertically or horizontally, resize them, and even choose whether a specific area should show a single app or a stack of them that you can flip through. To be clear, you can always have multiple apps in the same spot, it's more about how they're displayed.

This flexibility immediately makes FancyZones easy to recommend. I don't usually juggle a ton of apps at the same time, but I need them to be laid out in the ideal way. I usually have my research and writing windows side-by-side in relatively large sizes, and a smaller column for my messaging apps at the edge. But you can get far crazier than that.

4 reasons why I ditched Snap Assist for FancyZones

With FancyZones, I got more layout options and better multitasking support than Snap Assist ever offered.

1
By  Judy Sanhz

But then there's the other aspect, which is the ease of using these layouts in the first place. Unlike Snap Layouts, you don't need to carefully drag windows along the edges of the screen or open dedicated menus. Simply hold Shift (or another key of your choosing) and move the window around into the area where you want it to be. When you let go of the window, it will snap perfectly into position, and you're ready to go. You can also just keep dragging windows from one spot to another and it never resets your layout. You always have full freedom.

It's hard to imagine using a PC without this capability, to the point where even when I'm using another platform, such as macOS or Linux, I've had to find replacements to do the same thing.

You can save specific configurations, too

Plus keep apps on top

FancyZones may be the best part of PowerToys, but it's actually not the only trick up its sleeve when it comes to window management. Another tool included in PowerToys is Workspaces, and it;s cool because it lets you capture your app and window layout at any time and save it as a preset. That includes your visible windows, but also the minimized apps, too.

What this means is you can use FancyZones to set up your apps in the right place, then use Workspaces to capture that layout perfectly, and the next time you turn on your computer, you can launch that workspace, and all your apps will open in the position you saved them in using FancyZones. Of course, you can also keep adjust freely after that.

Another notable window management tool is the self-explanatory Always on Top. This allows you to take any app window and keep it on top of all other windows, even as you keep interacting with other apps.

But wait, there's more

Grab and Move is for everyone

Whether you like using more rigid layouts in FancyZones or not, sometimes, you may find yourself using a couple of standard floating windows that don't need to go into a specific zone. Or maybe all your apps are like that. Regardless, there's one more tool in PowerToys that caps off its window management capabilities beautifully.

It's called Grab and Move, and what it does is allow you to move and resize windows without having to specifically target the edges of that window. Typically, to drag a window, you'd need to click its title bar, but with Grab and Move, you can hold down a modifier key of your choosing, and then you can grab the window from anywhere and move it around. You don't even need to switch the focus to that window, either, Grab and Move lets you drag a window and move it behind another one.

PowerToys is Microsoft's test lab for the Windows features you actually want, and some have actually made it over

Testing the waters

1
By  João Carrasqueira

Similar, you can use a different modifier key to enable resizing without reaching for the edges of the window. Hold the key and click the ap's window anywhere, then drag in the direction you want to shrink or expand the window. You may not notice the extra couple of seconds it takes to properly align your mouse with the right are to resize a window, or even move it, but over time, you'll definitely feel faster and more productive using this feature.

PowerToys is fantastic

I've sung the praises of PowerToys many times in the past, but it always bears repeating. This is an absolutely essential app for any Windows user. You're probably not going to care for all of the features on offer, but there's so much packed into this relatively small package that almost everyone should find enough good to make it worth your time.

Window management alone is a great reason to love PowerToys, but you can throw in things like Command Palette or Power Display and the value really starts to add up. You can check it out below if you haven't already.

Microsoft PowerToys
OS
Windows 10/11

A lot of power in your pocket

A big inner screen that folds away

The main draw is the 7.6-inch main display you get when the phone is open. Its 4:3 shape leaves room to run two apps side by side, which suits reading an e-book or working through a spreadsheet. When the phone is closed, the 5.5-inch cover display handles quick texts and calls, so you only unfold it when you need the extra space. Under the hood, you get the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. The battery is 4800mAh, and Samsung rates it for up to 26 hours of video playback.

On the back, there's a 50MP wide camera and a 50MP ultra-wide. Samsung also lists 2x optical zoom and up to 10x digital zoom. For selfies and video calls, there's a 10MP camera on the cover screen and another on the main screen, so you can use whichever side of the phone is facing you.

The phone is 4.5mm thick when unfolded and weighs 7.1 ounces. Folded, it measures 123.9 x 81.9 x 9.7mm, and it opens up to 123.9 x 161.4mm. Samsung lists the Fold 8 in Pistachio, Lavender, Graphite, and Cream, and this sales price applies to all colors. Samsung also says some colors are exclusive to Samsung.com or its Experience Stores, so confirm that Amazon sells the color you want.

This phone makes the most sense if you read, write, or work on your phone a lot and want more screen without carrying a second device. The tablet-like size makes it a good replacement for work while still being phone-sized when you need it. If you mostly text, scroll, and take photos, a regular phone will do the job.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 review: The first foldable I don't want to put down

If you're willing to make a few spec-related compromises and are willing to drop the cash, this is the foldable to buy.

Over the past 90 days, the average price was $1,930.09. If you want a bigger screen without paying the full $2,099.99, grab the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 while it's on sale.

item.title: Physical media is the only ad-free tier left that never gets more expensive
item.itunes:title: Physical media is the only ad-free tier left that never gets more expensive
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
As we approach the end of the year, I wanted to audit my monthly household entertainment bills and quickly realized that maintaining ad-free 4K tiers across streaming services has quietly surpassed the cost of traditional cable packages.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Streaming platforms rely on recurring price adjustments and tier advertising in order to reach profitability. However, physical media, whether that's 4K UHD Blu-rays, standard Blu-rays, or even CDs, functions as a fixed-cost permanent license that avoids ongoing subscription inflation and mid-stream commercial interruptions.

Physical media isn't a complete replacement for the convenience and discovery that modern streaming provides. Instead, it's a fantastic hardware-backed hedge for high-rewatch-value titles, home theater enthusiasts, and users hoping to build local media servers. Year over year, streaming services are increasing in cost, so I needed to find an alternative.

Streaming services constantly increase their prices

And get rid of your favorite shows

Over the past two years, streaming service prices have hiked across major platforms, including Netflix, Disney Plus, Peacock, Apple TV, and Amazon Prime Video. Alongside higher prices, these platforms have widened the price gap between ad-supported and ad-free plans to drive users toward ad-tier revenue.

Recurring monthly fees, especially when they are increasing, can feel devastating compared to the one-time purchase cost of physical discs. Buying used Blu-rays or even waiting for standard retail sales can create a fixed amortization curve. By watching a $15 to $20 disc three or four times over several years, it lowers the per-view cost below a single month of a premium 4K streaming tier, with zero exposure to future rate hikes.

Alongside this, there's licensing stability with physical possession compared to digital storefront purchases. Even when buying a film or show digitally on services like Apple TV, Amazon Prime Video, or Fandango at Home, you don't actually own the piece of media itself. Instead, you get a revocable streaming license, subject to studio rights expirations and strict offline DRM checks, whereas with a physical disc it remains playable offline indefinitely without any server authentication.

With some discs, it can feel like there are ads because they occasionally include unskippable studio anti-piracy warnings or pre-menu trailers. But technically, these are different: they occur strictly before the root menu loads and never interrupt the feature presentation itself. They can even be bypassed entirely when backing up personal discs to a local server.

Every time a movie disappears from streaming, I'm glad I already own it on Blu-ray

Owning physical media can't be emphasized enough in a streaming age where movies vanish.

1
By  Brian Burgess

Physical media always wins out when it comes to bitrate

Streaming services don't look anywhere near as good

Alongside these issues comes the 4K technical gap. A 4K label on a streaming tier doesn't equal the same visual fidelity as a 4K UHD Blu-ray disc. Streaming platforms must prioritize smooth delivery over variable residential bandwidth, so they rely on aggressive compression.

Major platforms like Netflix and Prime Video typically deliver 4K streams at roughly 15 to 25Mbps, even with efficient codecs like HEVC and AV1. Higher-tier exceptions like Apple TV Plus reach up to 40 Mbps and Sony Pictures Core peaks at around 80Mbps. This bitrate differs significantly from that of physical disks, with standard 1080p Blu-rays routinely averaging 20 to 30Mbps.

4K UHD discs, which utilize 66 GB and 100 GB triple-layer capacities, operate at video bitrates between 40 Mbps and 144Mbps. Higher bit rates prevent macroblocking and posterization in dark shadow gradients and complex grain structures, creating a major visual impact when you're watching your media library.

Audio suffers even more than video on streaming platforms. Streaming services rely on lossy Dolby Digital Plus, capped at low bit rates, in order to conserve bandwidth, whereas Blu-ray and 4K UHD discs provide lossless object-based audio tracks like Dolby TrueHD with Atmos and DTS-HD Master Audio/DTS:X (delivering a noticeably wider dynamic range and low-end clarity on dedicated soundbars or AVR setups).

The self-hosted workflow

This can provide you with the convenience of streaming

There is a way to bridge physical ownership and modern convenience. One of the biggest sets of valid criticisms of physical media is swapping discs, slow Java-based Blu-ray menus, and lack of multi-room access. But local digitalization is the technical bridge that can give physical media the convenience of a private streaming service.

You can back up your discs for personal local use by picking up some optical hardware. Use an external or internal UHD-friendly optical drive flashed with LibreDrive firmware in order to read 4K BDXL discs cleanly. Not every drive is compatible, as the flash works only on specific models with specific firmware requirements. Make sure you check compatibility before buying.

You can then use tools like MakeMKV to remux the raw video, lossless audio, and subtitle tracks into a .mkv container, preserving 100% of the disc's original bitrate while stripping out pre-menu trailers and FBI warnings. You can then host these remuxes on a local NAS and serve them across your home TVs, tablets, and phones via self-hosted media servers like Plex or Jellyfin.

Keep in mind that a 1080p Blu-ray disc typically takes 20GB to 35GB, while a 4K UHD disc requires 50GB to 85 GB. Storage is expensive, and the upfront cost of high-capacity hard drives can feel steep. But compared to years of compounding subscription fees, it might be the better trade-off for you. Alongside this, the zero-cloud reliability means that, as your local media server backed by physical disks functions seamlessly during ISP outages, it requires zero monthly cloud fees and gives you complete control over the metadata, UI layout, and subtitle rendering.

I won't be canceling all of my streaming subscriptions

But some of them will be getting the boot

The smartest approach for tech-savvy consumers isn't canceling every streaming service outright but downgrading bloated multi-platform subscriptions to occasional rotating months for new releases. By dedicating a modest budget to physical discs for favorite films, reference-grade home theater showcases, and comfort shows, you're creating a permanent high-bitrate library.

Once a disc is paid for and sitting on a shelf (or even mirrored onto a local NAS), there's no corporate restructuring, licensing dispute, or quarterly earnings call that can take it away from you, insert a 90-second ad break into it, or even increase its price next year.

I spent $200 on thrifted 4K Blu-rays instead of digital rentals, and my local Plex library paid for itself in months

item.title: This two-decade old browser is still the best productivity tool in my workflow
item.itunes:title: This two-decade old browser is still the best productivity tool in my workflow
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've tried plenty of browsers over the years, often looking for something faster, cleaner, or better suited to my work. Yet Firefox has remained a constant in my setup for a reason. It isn't just about opening websites or keeping bookmarks organized. There's a surprising amount of functionality tucked inside this two-decade-old browser, and some of it has genuinely changed how I handle everyday tasks. I decided to take a closer look at what makes it so difficult to replace.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Customization options make it feel like my own productivity workspace

It lets me customize more than just the usual browser settings

Firefox offers plenty of customization options even before installing extensions or digging into advanced settings. It lets me rearrange toolbar buttons, remove unnecessary elements, customize the bookmarks toolbar, and choose which shortcuts and sections appear on the New Tab page. Mozilla also provides built-in themes, light and dark appearances, and wallpapers, including the option to use my own images. These small adjustments make the browser feel less like a fixed interface and more like a workspace I can organize around my daily activities.

Things get more interesting beyond these regular settings. Firefox's about:config page exposes hundreds of advanced preferences that aren't available in the standard settings menu, allowing experienced users to fine-tune browser behavior. There's also userChrome.css, which takes customization a step further by letting users modify the browser's actual interface using CSS. From changing tab appearances and toolbar spacing to hiding or repositioning interface elements, the possibilities go well beyond what most mainstream browsers offer. Mozilla doesn't officially support these advanced modifications, and updates can occasionally break them, but the flexibility is impressive.

Extensions like uBlock Origin help block unwanted content, while Sidebery introduces advanced tab management through a customizable sidebar. Combined with themes, keyboard shortcuts, and interface adjustments, Firefox offers enough flexibility to create a browsing environment that genuinely fits different working styles.

6 Firefox-based browsers that smoke Chrome

It's time to ditch Google

4
By  João Carrasqueira

Built-in privacy and account management features

Keep multiple online accounts separate without juggling browser profiles

Managing multiple online accounts can quickly become messy, especially when work and personal activities overlap. Firefox addresses this with its built-in Containers feature, which separates browsing sessions into color-coded tabs, each maintaining its own cookies and website data. This lets me keep work and personal Gmail accounts logged in simultaneously without opening separate browser profiles or repeatedly signing in and out. Mozilla's Multi-Account Containers extension builds on this functionality by allowing automatic website assignments and syncing container settings, including container names and website assignments, across devices.

That protection extends to email through Firefox Relay. It generates email masks that forward messages to a real inbox without exposing the primary email address. These aliases are handy when signing up for unfamiliar websites, newsletters, and online services.

Total Cookie Protection takes a different approach by automatically keeping cookies in separate, site-specific jars, making it harder for websites to track browsing activity across different sites. Enhanced Tracking Protection complements this by blocking known trackers and limiting unwanted tracking. Neither feature makes browsing completely anonymous, but together they offer better control over how websites collect information.

Features that make Firefox more than just a browser

It replaces several small tools in my daily workflow

Firefox's built-in PDF viewer and editor is perhaps the strongest example of how much functionality it packs beyond browsing. Instead of opening another application, I can highlight text, add comments, draw annotations, fill interactive forms, and insert saved signatures directly into PDFs from the browser. Keep in mind that these signatures are simply annotations, not legally binding e-signatures, and don't include authentication or verification. I regularly review PDFs while researching software, so these tools save me a few unnecessary steps. It isn't a replacement for advanced PDF editors, but it handles everyday document work surprisingly well.

Research also becomes easier with Firefox Translations and Reader View. The former translates supported webpages directly on-device without sending their content to an external translation service. Reader View removes advertisements, navigation elements, and other distractions, leaving a clean reading layout. Both are handy when going through lengthy articles and documentation.

The built-in screenshot tool is another welcome addition. It captures selected portions of webpages or entire pages, making it convenient to save visual references. Picture-in-Picture takes multitasking further by keeping videos in floating windows while I browse other tabs. It's particularly helpful when following software tutorials or product demonstrations without constantly switching windows.

A few smaller utilities round out the experience. Search shortcuts let me search specific websites directly from the address bar, while the Developer Tools eyedropper picks exact colors from webpages. Firefox's AI chatbot sidebar also provides access to supported AI assistants without leaving the current tab. Individually, these tools might seem minor, but together they make everyday tasks easier without relying on a collection of separate applications.

I ditched Firefox for this simple, non-AI browser, and I wish I’d done it sooner

Firefox had been my default for years, but this customizable browser made switching surprisingly easy.

2
By  Yash Patel

Not every upgrade needs a new application

I'm always interested in trying new tools, but the latest release isn't necessarily the best fit for every workflow. Firefox reminded me that familiar software can still surprise you when you explore it beyond the basics. I don't see a reason to replace something that continues to deliver value just for the sake of trying something newer. After all, productivity is about working smarter, not constantly rebuilding your toolkit.

item.title: 3 Home Assistant automations that use power draw instead of timers to control your dumb appliances
item.itunes:title: 3 Home Assistant automations that use power draw instead of timers to control your dumb appliances
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Traditional time-based automations in Home Assistant rely heavily on fixed delays, such as assuming a washing machine cycle takes precisely 45 minutes. This can fail when you factor in features like eco-modes, half loads, or unexpected operational pauses.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

By replacing time-based assumptions with real-time power-draw metrics from energy-monitoring smart plugs, I ensured Home Assistant could track exact device states based on physical and electrical output. I switched over three practical, hands-on Home Assistant automations that utilized power draw thresholds instead of timers in order to reliably control dumb appliances around my home and get accurate notifications, safety cutoffs, and energy tracking.

I replaced my smart bulbs with smart relays and saved my family from home automation fatigue

Your smart home shouldn't cause friction.

42
By  Jasmine Mannan

Washing machines and dryers

With a range of modes, these can be hard to time

It's difficult to use a timer for washing machines and dryers because they have complex operating profiles with varying cycle lengths, water-heating phases, and periodic pauses between washing and spinning stages that can make static timers unreliable.

By using an energy-monitoring smart plug, Home Assistant could track active wattage to detect distinct operational states, including standby, active running, mid-cycle pausing, and completion. The automation triggered when my power sensor's value crossed an upper threshold of 5W to flag that a cycle had officially started. To prevent false completions during brief mid-cycle pauses where power consumption drops to zero, I added a "for at least" delay condition (5 minutes below 2W) that must be met before triggering.

Once that power draw remains flat at baseline standby levels for the duration of the delay, Home Assistant then dispatches a notification to my phone and also announces via smart speaker that the laundry is ready. You can also set it up to send a persistent notification to your HA interface.

Coffee machines are tricky to automate

You don't want to accidentally cut power when you don't even have your coffee yet

Standard drip coffee machines or manual espresso machines lack automatic shut-off features or sometimes rely on generic countdowns that either cut power while the pot is still being kept warm on a burner or keep heating elements energized long after brewing has actually finished. By monitoring the distinct power-draw signature of a heating element, Home Assistant can dynamically differentiate between an active brew cycle, a low-draw keep-warm state, and complete inactivity.

The automation I set up uses a numeric state trigger that looks for a sudden surge in wattage exceeding 800W when the heating element engages. Upon detecting the initial heating spike followed by a drop to a lower sustained draw (the warming plate phase, which is 50 W), Home Assistant starts tracking how long the secondary draw persists without requiring an arbitrary hard-coded clock.

When the power draw drops to 2W for more than 15 minutes (which signifies that the brew cycle is finished), the smart plug cuts power entirely, mitigating fire hazards and saving idle energy.

This Home Assistant integration makes your dumb washing machine smart

Turning dumb appliances into smart objects.

8
By  Rich Edmonds

A dehumidifier can be hard to keep track of

Full water tanks can cause issues

Portable basement dehumidifiers run on intermittent compressor cycles dictated by ambient humidity levels, but this can make it impossible to predict when their water collection buckets will fill up and force an automatic shutdown. Rather than guessing when a tank is full based on elapsed operating hours, an energy monitoring plug can track the active compressor load versus the dehumidifier's standby state.

Under normal operating conditions, my dehumidifier draws a consistent high wattage of around 200W as the compressor and fan run concurrently. However, when the physical water tank fills up, the internal float switch cuts power to the compressor, causing the overall power draw to abruptly drop to a low power state of 2W while the unit's error light blinks.

Home Assistant captures this specific drop and waits until it lasts over 30 minutes to ensure it's because the tank is full, not just because the room reached the target humidity, then sends an actionable notification to my phone to empty the water reservoir and prevent potential overflows. This will, of course, vary based on what dehumidifier you have and applies to my unit specifically.

Real-time wattage thresholds provide so much intel

Switching from rigid, time-based timers to dynamic power-draw logic can turn standard non-smart appliances into responsive nodes within Home Assistant. It takes your standard dumb appliances and turns them into what feels like smart appliances without the attached inflated price tag. By evaluating real-time wattage thresholds and incorporating stabilizing time delays, you can eliminate false triggers caused by operational pauses too.

This telemetry-driven methodology ensures notifications arrive precisely when chores finish, safety shut-offs occur reliably, and overall home automation robustness is significantly improved. Make sure you check your smart plug's rating before using it with high-draw appliances, as dryers and some kettles or espresso machines can draw close to a typical plug's rated limit.

If you're looking for a smart plug that can monitor energy states, then the Tapo P110 is a great option.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Budget security cameras usually ask you to trade video quality for a low price. The Blink Mini 2K+ narrows that gap, and Amazon has it for $15.99, down from $39.99, as part of a Black Friday deal.

Brand
Blink

The Blink Mini 2K+ is a compact plug-in indoor security camera that records up to 2K video and works without a Sync Module. It has a 138° diagonal field of view, infrared night vision, and two-way audio with a built-in siren.

See at Amazon

Cheap and capable, with a few limits

Sharp 2K video from a tiny indoor camera

You get video up to 2K at 16:9, plus 1080p Standard and 720p Saver modes that need less upload speed. The field of view is 138° diagonal, and the camera measures 2 by 2 inches and 1.57 inches deep (51 mm by 51 mm by 40 mm). It weighs 65 grams, not counting the cable.

The Wi-Fi radio is 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6), but it's limited to the 2.4 GHz band, so it won't join a 5 GHz network. It supports WPA, WPA2, and WPA3, and Blink recommends WPA3. Blink lists minimum upload speeds of 6 Mbps for 2K, 3 Mbps for Standard, and 2 Mbps for Saver, so check your connection before you count on the top quality mode working. If your 2.4 GHz signal is weak where the camera will sit, the lower modes serve as a fallback.

Power comes from a 5V USB-C supply, and the camera is built primarily for indoor use. The IP65 rating applies only when connected to Blink's optional weather-resistant power adapter, sold separately. Per camera, Blink lists an indoor-rated power supply, a 2m USB-C cable, a wall mount or base, and two mounting screws included in the box.

The bigger catch is Blink's ecosystem. Person and vehicle detection is available only with a Blink Subscription Plan. Also, the camera can't save video, so you'll need certain Sync Modules or the Blink Subscription Plan to save footage. If you'd rather keep everything on your own hardware, sort that out before you buy. So, the Mini 2K+ is a good fit if you like to tinker and want an inexpensive indoor camera for a room or two, but a weaker one if you want detection features without a plan.

The $39.99 list price is well above most of Amazon's monthly lows this year, so the 60% savings flatters the deal a little. Even so, it's a low price for a camera with 2K video, and we think it's worth a look if Blink's ecosystem suits you. You can pick up the Blink Mini 2K+ while it lasts.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
One of the most frequent tasks I do is transfer files from one device to another. I take a lot of photos on my OnePlus 15 that I need to edit on my Windows PC. I also need to share screenshots from my partner's iPhone or MacBook to my PC, so having a dependable file-sharing solution becomes necessary. I had been using email or multiple third-party apps till now, but then I discovered PairDrop, an open-source, browser-based, P2P file-sharing tool.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Instead of installing yet another app on every single device, PairDrop allows me to simply open a browser tab and instantly send files to any other device on the same network. I don't even need to pair devices before transferring files. I had come across apps like LocalSend, but I prefer this app-less, cross-platform solution now. The speed is limited only by my network, and the process is as seamless as it can be.

I stopped emailing files to myself after discovering this open-source AirDrop killer

It's cross-platform and way faster

By  Patrick Hearn

PairDrop works entirely in your web browser

No app installs, no ads, and no limits

The joy of solving a recurring problem without installing a new app is underrated. I already have too many programs on my PC, and more apps than I need on my phone. Transferring files from my phone or my partner's phone to my PC is something I do almost every day, since I need to click photos for my articles. This necessitates a permanent solution, so you might think that I'd choose a decent app and call it a day.

However, discovering PairDrop made me realize that I didn't need another app. This tool works in a browser tab, connecting to any recipient device on the same network. My browser is always open on my PC and phone, so there's no friction when initiating a transfer. PairDrop uses WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication) to create a direct link between the browsers; nothing is uploaded to the cloud, and DTLS encryption keeps your data safe.

Before finding out about PairDrop, I relied on apps like Send Anywhere, which had a ton of ads. PairDrop has a clean UI, no ads, and no transfer limits. It's basically the perfect way to shuttle data from one device to another.

These 4 free AirDrop alternatives made file sharing on Android effortless

Moving files on Android became effortless with these powerful sharing tools.

By  Yash Patel

I can easily share files with my partner's Apple devices

From my Windows PC or Android phone

While I had my chosen app for the Android-to-Windows part of the problem, I often struggled with sending files to and from my partner's iMac, MacBook, and iPhone. The Apple ecosystem works well for the devices inside it, but not for everything else. PairDrop is a cross-platform tool that covers Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS, so I never have to think about the OS on a device anymore. A browser window and two devices on the same network are all I need.

I've bookmarked Pairdrop.net on every device in the house, so it's always just a click away. I tap on the required device on the screen and choose the files I need to transfer. The person on the other end approves the transfer, and it's done. While the receiver needs to stay on the PairDrop browser tab till the prompt pops up, it's a minor downside to an otherwise excellent tool.

Besides, I rarely need to send files to my partner without telling her, so the risk of her missing out on the prompt isn't as common as some people might think. If the sender and receiver are on different networks, PairDrop allows simple pairing to establish a connection. And the option to join a temporary public room enables more people to share files with each other.

I tried replacing Quick Share with LocalSend, PairDrop, and Blip — only one became my go-to

Three apps, dozens of file transfers, and one clear winner that finally replaced Quick Share for me.

7
By  Yash Patel

It's blazing-fast and open-source

What's not to like?

Sending a handful of photos from a phone to a PC doesn't take much time, but large files need ample transfer speeds to reduce the waiting time. Fortunately, PairDrop's maximum throughput depends only on your network speed, after accounting for hardware and device overhead. During my testing, PairDrop reached around 20 MB/s, which is roughly in line with my maximum network speed (200 Mbps).

The best part about PairDrop is that it's open-source, so you don't need to trust an organization not to see or store your data. PairDrop transfers happen directly between the devices, and you can verify the source code on GitHub. While LocalSend is also open-source, it's an additional app to install. And the popular Blip app isn't open-source, so PairDrop has more than a few things going for it.

I ditched Dropbox after finding this free self-hosted file-sharing app, and I'm not going back

Syncthing replaced my Dropbox subscription, and it syncs straight between my devices

By  Ayush Pande

PairDrop seems magical, but this is what file-sharing should be like

People shouldn't be forced to pay just to share files between their own devices. PairDrop makes cross-platform file-sharing as simple and seamless as possible. You don't even need to install anything. Your devices only need to be on the same network, and PairDrop will do the rest. It's an ad-free tool with no data limits, and it deserves a spot on your browser's bookmark list.

Pairdrop
See at Pairdrop See at Github

PairDrop works entirely in your web browser

No app installs, no ads, and no limits

The joy of solving a recurring problem without installing a new app is underrated. I already have too many programs on my PC, and more apps than I need on my phone. Transferring files from my phone or my partner's phone to my PC is something I do almost every day, since I need to click photos for my articles. This necessitates a permanent solution, so you might think that I'd choose a decent app and call it a day.

However, discovering PairDrop made me realize that I didn't need another app. This tool works in a browser tab, connecting to any recipient device on the same network. My browser is always open on my PC and phone, so there's no friction when initiating a transfer. PairDrop uses WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication) to create a direct link between the browsers; nothing is uploaded to the cloud, and DTLS encryption keeps your data safe.

Before finding out about PairDrop, I relied on apps like Send Anywhere, which had a ton of ads. PairDrop has a clean UI, no ads, and no transfer limits. It's basically the perfect way to shuttle data from one device to another.

It's blazing-fast and open-source

What's not to like?

Sending a handful of photos from a phone to a PC doesn't take much time, but large files need ample transfer speeds to reduce the waiting time. Fortunately, PairDrop's maximum throughput depends only on your network speed, after accounting for hardware and device overhead. During my testing, PairDrop reached around 20 MB/s, which is roughly in line with my maximum network speed (200 Mbps).

The best part about PairDrop is that it's open-source, so you don't need to trust an organization not to see or store your data. PairDrop transfers happen directly between the devices, and you can verify the source code on GitHub. While LocalSend is also open-source, it's an additional app to install. And the popular Blip app isn't open-source, so PairDrop has more than a few things going for it.
